passage.bullet: Steep mountains sliced mainland Greece into narrow valleys → slow mountain tracks kept towns apart
Over a thousand Aegean islands lay scattered offshore → separating towns across open water
Towns formed rival poleis like Athens and Sparta → guarding their own laws and coins

context.bullet: Earlier Minoan island palaces and Mycenaean hilltop forts → already grew as separate regional strongholds
Wooden boats beat carts over rocky mountain tracks → Greeks travelled faster by sea

stems.stem: Across the Greek mainland, steep ____________ and narrow valleys meant towns remained ____________.
Scattered across the ____________ Sea, over a thousand ____________ stopped Greece becoming one single kingdom.
Because travel between valleys was slow, independent ____________ such as ____________ and ____________ made their own laws and coins.

lesson_1.watch_out: Ancient Greece was never one single united country under one king—it was a patchwork of rival independent city-states called poleis.

passage.bullet: Walled Acropolis rose high above town roofs → sheltered families safely whenever enemy armies attacked
Citizens built marble temples atop the Acropolis → honoured the patron god protecting their polis
Sunny lowland Agora hosted food and pottery stalls → men gathered daily to debate laws

context.bullet: Rival poleis often clashed over border land → cities needed hilltop walls against sudden raids
Morning arguments in the open Agora → planted early habits of public debate and voting

stems.stem: High above the city roofs, the walled ____________ protected families from attack and held marble ____________.
Down on flat ground, farmers and potters used the open ____________ to sell ____________ and painted clay bowls.
Together, the high city gave a polis ____________ and worship, while the busy marketplace handled ____________ and political debate.

lesson_1.watch_out: Do not mix up the two Greek names—the Acropolis was the high fortified temple hill, whereas the Agora was the flat open marketplace below.

passage.bullet: Greeks called themselves Hellenes → spoke one shared language and worshipped the same Olympian gods
Greeks adapted Phoenician signs into a twenty-four-letter alphabet → vowels let towns carve readable laws
Ships exported olive oil and painted jars → brought home vital wheat for rocky towns

context.bullet: Rocky mountain slopes grew little wheat → farmers planted hardy olive trees and grapevines instead
Common speech and Olympian gods → later drew rival poleis together at pan-Greek festivals

stems.stem: Even though rival poleis fought, Greeks called themselves ____________ and shared one ____________ and religion.
Around 800 BC, sea traders adapted ____________ signs by adding vowels to create the twenty-four-letter ____________.
Because rocky hillsides had thin soil, ships swapped Greek ____________ and ____________ overseas for vital wheat grain.

lesson_1.watch_out: Ancient Greeks did not call themselves Greeks—they called themselves Hellenes and named their homeland Hellas, sharing culture rather than one government.

passage.bullet: Adult male citizens met on the Pnyx hill → voted by hand on every law
Ostrakon shards banished bossy leaders → kleroterion machines picked five hundred jurors fairly by chance
Athenian democracy barred women, enslaved people, and foreign metics → most adults had zero vote

context.bullet: Sea trade drew foreign metics to Athens → they worked in the polis without voting
Daily debates in the open Agora → prepared male citizens to argue on the Pnyx

stems.stem: On the rocky ____________ hill, adult male citizens debated laws themselves and raised hands in ____________.
To stop cheats or tyrants, voters scratched names on ____________ shards and chose jurors using a marble ____________.
Despite calling their system people-power, Athens excluded ____________, ____________, and foreign-born ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Athenian direct democracy was very different from modern voting—citizens voted on every law in person, yet women, enslaved people, and metics were completely excluded.

passage.bullet: Two kings ruled beside older nobles → Sparta prized strict obedience over open debate
Conquered helots worked the fields → freed Spartan citizen men to train full-time for war
Seven-year-old boys entered the harsh agoge → went barefoot, slept on reeds, and practised stealth

context.bullet: Ringed inland by steep mountains → Sparta built land armies rather than sea-trading fleets
Helot farmworkers outnumbered Spartan citizens → fear of rebellion drove Sparta’s tough military lifestyle

stems.stem: Unlike democratic Athens, inland Sparta was led by ____________ alongside a council of ____________, relying on conquered ____________ to farm.
Once a Spartan boy turned ____________, he left home for the ____________ to build toughness and obedience.
Inside the barracks, boys walked ____________ in winter, slept on ____________, and ate thin dark broth.

lesson_2.watch_out: Sparta did not have one single all-powerful king—two kings ruled side by side with a council of older nobles so neither king held total control.

passage.bullet: Athenian girls rarely attended school → stayed indoors learning weaving under male guardians
Spartan girls trained outdoors in running and wrestling → fit mothers raised strong soldiers
Husbands lived in barracks → Spartan women owned land, ran estates, and spoke publicly

context.bullet: Wealthy Athenian boys studied reading, geometry, and speechmaking → preparing for Pnyx debates
Even in freer Sparta → women still could not sit on councils or command armies

stems.stem: Inside wealthy Athenian households, boys studied with tutors while girls stayed indoors learning ____________ under male ____________.
Outdoors in Sparta, girls practised ____________, wrestling, and javelin because citizens believed strong mothers raised ____________.
Because Spartan husbands lived away in ____________, Spartan women could own ____________ and manage farms themselves.

lesson_2.watch_out: Do not assume Athens gave women more freedom because it was a democracy—Spartan women actually owned land and exercised outdoors far more freely than Athenian women.

passage.bullet: Twelve Olympian gods ruled from Mount Olympus → governing forces like thunder, seas, and wisdom
Cities built marble temples like the Parthenon → sheltered towering statues of their patron god
Worshippers gathered outdoors at stone altars → poured wine and burned meat offerings for gods

context.bullet: Athens built its marble Parthenon high on the Acropolis → visible to sailors miles offshore
Rival poleis chose different patron gods → yet all Hellenes honoured Zeus’s Olympian family

stems.stem: Greeks believed twelve immortal gods ruled from snowy ____________, led by thunderbolt-hurling ____________ and queen ____________.
To honour their patron goddess, Athenians built the marble ____________ housing a huge gold-and-ivory statue of ____________.
Rather than praying quietly inside, crowds stood outdoors at stone ____________ to pour ____________ and roast meat.

lesson_3.watch_out: Greek temples like the Parthenon were not churches where crowds sat inside—temples housed the god’s statue, while citizens worshipped outdoors around smoky stone altars.

passage.bullet: Generals and sailors climbed Delphi before big decisions → priestess Pythia spoke Apollo’s mysterious riddles
Poets chanted myths of Heracles and Odysseus → taught bravery and wit through monster quests
Potters painted black-figure and red-figure myths on jars → brought hero stories to supper tables

context.bullet: Merchant ships traded painted Greek pottery abroad → carried Olympian myths across the sea
Handwritten papyrus scrolls stayed rare and costly → spoken songs and painted vases taught everyone

stems.stem: Before launching wars or voyages, Greek leaders climbed ____________ to hear riddles spoken by the priestess ____________.
Chanted myths kept beliefs alive through tales of ____________ battling the Hydra and ____________ outwitting giants.
Craftworkers decorated glossy ____________ and ____________ clay vases so everyday jars retold famous sacred stories.

lesson_3.watch_out: The Pythia at Delphi never gave plain yes-or-no instructions—she spoke puzzling riddles from Apollo that kings and generals could easily misread.

passage.bullet: Messengers declared a Sacred Truce across Greece → paused wars so athletes travelled safely
Athletes swore fair-play oaths to Zeus → raced barefoot and competed in wrestling and chariots
Winners wore a wild-olive kotinos crown → earned lasting glory for their home polis

context.bullet: Sunny Olympia lay in southern Greece → far away from snowy Mount Olympus
Only Greek-speaking Hellenes competed together at Olympia → strengthened shared identity across rival city-states

stems.stem: Every four summers from ____________, messengers announced the ____________ so warring city-states paused fighting for safe travel.
At the shrine of ____________, athletes swore beside ____________ never to cheat before racing in the stadion and chariots.
Instead of gold or silver medals, Olympic champions wore a wild-olive ____________ to bring glory to their ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Do not confuse Olympia with Mount Olympus—the Olympic Games took place at the valley shrine of Olympia in southern Greece, not on top of snowy Mount Olympus—and winners wore olive wreaths, never gold medals.

passage.bullet: Athenian citizen hoplites locked bronze shields and spears together → formed an unbroken fighting phalanx
Greek phalanx charged fast across Marathon plain → smashed lighter Persian archers at close range
Legend says Pheidippides ran twenty-six miles to warn Athens → inspired today’s long-distance marathon race

context.bullet: Athenian hoplites defended their young democracy → voted themselves to march out rather than surrender
Vast Persian Empire ruled millions under King Darius → expected one small polis to surrender

stems.stem: When Persian King ____________ invaded in 490 BC to punish Athens, his archers landed on the plain of ____________.
Locking bronze shields and long spears into a tight ____________, citizen ____________ charged fast to break Persian lines.
Athenians buried fallen soldiers beneath a grassy ____________, while ____________’s twenty-six-mile run inspired the modern marathon.

lesson_4.watch_out: Spartan soldiers did not win the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC—Athenian citizen hoplites defeated Darius’s Persians before Sparta’s army arrived.

passage.bullet: Steep cliffs and crashing sea squeezed Thermopylae narrow → cancelled out King Xerxes’s huge numbers
Leonidas’s Spartans and Greek allies locked shields → held off elite Immortals for three days
A traitor showed Xerxes a mountain track → Leonidas stayed behind so Greek allies escaped

context.bullet: Harsh agoge training from age seven → prepared Leonidas’s Spartans never to break ranks
Old rivals Sparta and Athens united in 480 BC → defended Hellene freedom together

stems.stem: Squeezed between steep ____________ and the sea, the narrow pass of ____________ stopped Xerxes using his huge numbers.
Led by Spartan King ____________, three hundred Spartans and Greek allies held back the Persian ____________ for three days.
Once a traitor revealed a secret ____________, Leonidas stayed fighting to buy time for ____________ to retreat.

lesson_4.watch_out: Thermopylae was a heroic Persian victory rather than a Greek win, and the three hundred Spartans did not fight completely alone—thousands of other Greek allies guarded the pass beside them.

passage.bullet: Themistocles sent Xerxes a trick message → lured the Persian fleet into narrow Salamis
Narrow strait jammed Persian warships together → crowded crews crashed without room to turn
Fast triremes rowed by 170 oarsmen → smashed trapped Persian hulls with waterline bronze rams

context.bullet: Families evacuated Athens before Persians burned it → saved lives while warships fought offshore
Winning at Salamis and Plataea kept Greece free → sparked Athens’s golden age of culture

stems.stem: Trusting fast wooden ____________ rowed by 170 oarsmen, Admiral ____________ relied on speed and heavy ____________ rams.
By sending King Xerxes a ____________, the Greeks lured the massive Persian fleet into the narrow ____________.
Jammed inside tight waters, big Persian ships ____________ together while nimble Greek warships rammed them to save ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Greek triremes did not sink enemy ships with cannons or gunpowder—three tiers of oarsmen rowed fast to smash enemy hulls with a heavy bronze ram at the waterline.

passage.bullet: Curved hillside stone rows at Epidaurus → carried actors’ whispers clearly to fourteen thousand spectators
Actors wore bold wide-mouthed masks → back rows spotted sad tragedies and funny comedies
City coin tokens let poor citizens attend → everyone watched and debated justice together

context.bullet: Tragedies explored pride, duty, and tough moral choices → sharpened citizens’ judgement for Pnyx votes
Plays honoured Olympian wine-god Dionysus → theatre grew directly out of public religious festivals

stems.stem: Carved into sunny hillsides like ____________, curved stone rows carried clear voices to ____________ spectators without microphones.
During festivals for ____________, male actors wore exaggerated ____________ to perform serious ____________ and lively comedies.
Giving coin tokens to ____________ meant theatre united citizens to reflect on justice and human choices.

lesson_5.watch_out: Ancient Greek theatres had no electric lights, roofs, or female actors—performances happened in bright daylight, and male actors switched painted masks to play every male and female character.

passage.bullet: Barefoot Socrates questioned citizens daily in the Agora → pushed Athenians to test unproven beliefs
Condemned by jurors in 399 BC, Socrates drank poison → refused to abandon honest questioning
Aristotle observed and grouped hundreds of plants and animals → built early roots for science

context.bullet: Plato preserved Socrates’s talks at Athens’s Academy → taught young Aristotle before Aristotle’s own Lyceum
Aristotle’s wide learning → soon made him royal tutor to young Alexander of Macedon

stems.stem: Walking barefoot through the ____________, ____________ became famous for asking sharp questions that tested citizens’ beliefs.
After Socrates died in 399 BC, his pupil ____________ founded the Academy and taught young ____________.
At his ____________ school, Aristotle advanced science by ____________, measuring, and grouping real plants and animals.

lesson_5.watch_out: Socrates never wrote a single book himself—we know his famous questioning method because his devoted pupil Plato wrote down their conversations afterward.

passage.bullet: Hippocrates studied natural symptoms and bedside notes → replaced magic cures with careful observation
Hippocrates’s ethical Oath bound doctors to help patients → shaped medical duty for centuries
Pythagoras and Euclid unlocked triangle and geometry rules → Archimedes mastered levers and water displacement

context.bullet: Sick Greeks once blamed illnesses on angry gods → checking natural causes transformed healing
Exact Greek geometry and lever maths → helped engineers raise balanced marble temples and lighthouses

stems.stem: Instead of blaming angry gods for sickness, ____________ on Kos observed natural ____________ and kept bedside notes.
Prescribing clean food and rest, Greek doctors promised to care ethically for patients under the ____________.
While ____________ studied triangles and ____________ wrote a geometry guide, ____________ mastered levers and shouted Eureka!

lesson_5.watch_out: Hippocrates did not discover modern germs or antibiotics—his breakthrough was observing natural bodily symptoms and patient care instead of blaming angry gods.

passage.bullet: Crowned king of Macedon in 336 BC → young Alexander united Greece before marching east
Bold cavalry charges rode undefeated for eleven years → conquered Egypt, Persia, and north-west India
New Alexandria cities mixed Greek speech with eastern customs → created the connected Hellenistic world

context.bullet: Philosopher Aristotle tutored young Prince Alexander → inspired him to carry Greek learning east
Persia had once invaded Greece at Marathon and Salamis → Alexander now conquered Persia itself

stems.stem: Tutored as a prince by ____________ and riding ____________, Alexander became king of ____________ aged twenty.
Over eleven unbeaten years from 336 BC, his armies marched across ____________, ____________, and north-west ____________.
By founding cities named ____________ that mixed Greek speech with local customs, he shaped the ____________ era.

lesson_6.watch_out: Alexander the Great was not born in Athens or Sparta—he ruled the northern kingdom of Macedon before uniting the Greek city-states under his command.

passage.bullet: Alexandria’s Great Library held vast papyrus scrolls → scholars studied stars, maps, and Euclid’s geometry
Roman legions conquered mainland Greece in 146 BC → ended independent rule for old poleis
Dazzled Romans copied marble statues, hired Greek tutors, and matched their own gods to Olympians

context.bullet: Alexander’s conquests made Greek an international language → let distant scholars share scrolls in Egypt
Rome carried Greek myths, columns, and poetry across Europe → preserved Hellene ideas for Britain

stems.stem: Beside the tall ____________ in Egypt, scholars inside Alexandria’s ____________ studied stars, maps, and geometry on papyrus scrolls.
Although tough legions from the ____________ conquered mainland Greece in ____________, Greek culture did not disappear.
Wealthy Romans copied Greek ____________, hired ____________ for their children, and matched Roman gods to Mount Olympus.

lesson_6.watch_out: Alexandria’s famous Great Library and Pharos Lighthouse stood in Egypt on the North African coast, not on the Greek mainland—and Roman conquest spread Greek ideas rather than erasing them.

passage.bullet: Modern elections and twelve-person courtroom juries → echo Athens’s bold experiments in citizen democracy
Everyday English words like school and planet join Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns on public buildings
Fourteen nations gathered in Athens in 1896 → revived Olympia’s festival as the Modern Olympics

context.bullet: Unlike Athens’s male-only Pnyx votes → modern democracy gives women and all adults equal votes
Modern Olympic marathons still cover twenty-six miles → remembering Pheidippides’s legendary run in 490 BC

stems.stem: Whenever citizens vote in elections or serve on ____________, we see the lasting legacy of Athenian ____________.
Greek roots live on in everyday words like ____________ and ____________, alongside Doric, Ionic, and ____________ columns.
In ____________, athletes from fourteen nations met inside Athens’s marble stadium to launch the ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Modern democracy improved on ancient Athens rather than copying it identically—today adults elect representatives and women have equal voting rights, unlike the male-only Pnyx.
